name: Emotional Intelligence Test
tagline: Measure how well you recognise, understand and manage emotions.
intro: Emotional intelligence is the ability to notice emotions, understand where they come from, manage them well and use them to build good relationships. This test looks at four areas: perceiving, understanding and regulating emotions, and handling emotions with other people. Answer honestly based on how you usually are, not how you would like to be. It takes about five minutes.
seoTitle: Emotional Intelligence Test – Free EQ test online
seoDescription: How emotionally intelligent are you? Take this free 5-minute EQ test on perceiving, understanding and managing emotions and get practical tips.

perceiving.name: Perceiving emotions
perceiving.short: How well you notice emotions in yourself and in others.
perceiving.low: Your answers suggest that emotions, your own and other people's, sometimes go unnoticed until they become strong. You may be more focused on facts and tasks than on feelings, which has its own advantages. Still, noticing emotions early gives you more choice in how to respond. Try a quick check-in a few times a day: what am I feeling right now, and where do I feel it in my body? In conversations, pay extra attention to tone of voice and facial expressions.
perceiving.mid: You notice emotions reasonably well, in yourself and in others, though subtle signals may sometimes slip past you, especially when you are busy or stressed. This is a solid base to build on. One tip: when you sense a shift in someone's mood, check it gently, for example by asking how they are really doing. For yourself, try naming your feelings more precisely than just 'good' or 'bad'. A wider emotional vocabulary sharpens your perception.
perceiving.high: You are highly attuned to emotions. You tend to notice your own feelings early and pick up on moods, tension and unspoken signals in others. This sensitivity helps you respond with care and avoid misunderstandings. Keep using it, but be aware that noticing everything can also be tiring. Remember that your read of others is a hypothesis, not a fact, so check before you act on it. Give yourself time to recharge after emotionally intense situations.

understanding.name: Understanding emotions
understanding.short: How well you understand the causes and course of emotions.
understanding.low: Your answers suggest that emotions can feel confusing at times, as if they come out of nowhere or are hard to explain. That is a common experience and a skill you can develop. Try keeping a short mood diary for a few weeks: note what you felt, what happened just before and how the feeling changed. Patterns will soon appear. Reading novels or watching films with attention to the characters' feelings can also deepen your understanding of others.
understanding.mid: You have a fair understanding of why emotions arise and how they develop, both in yourself and in others. Some reactions may still puzzle you, especially mixed or intense ones. One tip: when a feeling surprises you, ask yourself what need or value it might be protecting. Anger often points to a boundary, sadness to a loss. Discussing situations afterwards with a friend can also help you see emotional patterns more clearly.
understanding.high: You have a deep understanding of emotions. You can usually explain why you feel what you feel, foresee how situations will affect people and recognise the hurt or fear that may hide behind anger. This insight helps you make wiser decisions and support others well. Keep using it generously, but remember that understanding a feeling is not the same as having to fix it. Sometimes people simply need to be heard, not analysed.

regulating.name: Regulating emotions
regulating.short: How well you manage your emotions and recover from setbacks.
regulating.low: Your answers suggest that strong emotions can take the lead at times, making it hard to calm down or let go once you are upset. This is not a weakness of character; regulation is a skill that can be practised. Start with a simple pause: when you notice a strong feeling, breathe slowly for a minute before reacting. Regular sleep, exercise and moments of rest also make emotions easier to manage. If this feels very hard, a coach or therapist can help.
regulating.mid: You manage your emotions reasonably well most of the time, though stress, fatigue or certain triggers may still get the better of you occasionally. That is very human. Identify the two or three situations in which you most often lose your balance and plan a response in advance, such as taking a short break or postponing a difficult conversation. Healthy routines like movement and enough sleep strengthen your ability to stay steady.
regulating.high: You are skilled at managing your emotions. You can calm yourself, recover from disappointments and stay composed under pressure, which makes you reliable in difficult moments. Keep it up, and check that regulating does not turn into suppressing. Feelings that are always pushed aside tend to come back in other ways. Make sure you also have safe places and people with whom you can express what you feel, including the less comfortable emotions.

social.name: Relationship skills
social.short: How well you use emotions to connect, support and resolve conflicts with others.
social.low: Your answers suggest that handling emotions in relationships, such as comforting someone, managing tension or keeping friendships going, can be challenging for you. Many of these skills are learnable. Try starting with listening: when someone shares a problem, first summarise what you heard and how they seem to feel before offering advice. In conflicts, use 'I' statements to describe your own feelings rather than blaming. Small steps like these make a noticeable difference.
social.mid: You get along well with people in most situations and can offer support and handle disagreements reasonably well. Some situations, such as strong conflicts or very emotional conversations, may still feel difficult. One tip: before a tricky conversation, think about what the other person might feel and need, not just what you want to say. Afterwards, reflect briefly on what went well. This habit steadily strengthens your relationship skills.
social.high: You are skilled at using emotions to build and maintain relationships. People feel comfortable with you, you can ease tension and you know how to give support and feedback in a kind way. This makes you a valued friend, partner and colleague. Keep it up, and watch your own limits: people who are good at caring for others are often asked to do so a lot. Make sure your relationships also give you support in return.

summary: Emotional intelligence consists of several skills that work together. Below you see how you score on each of the four areas; higher scores mean stronger emotional skills. Your results are based on self-assessment, describe tendencies rather than fixed abilities, and every skill can be developed with practice.
